subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 13 periods = 520 minutes
Total: 13 periods · 8h 40min

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Try to make a model Q1–Q5 + Discussion, p.1
tasks_in_class.description: Make a model of buildings using blocks; answer: what parts shown, why selected, what shapes, how similar/different, what if one piece removed.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Project Work, p.2
tasks_in_class.description: Observe a Qutub Minar model; answer what shape to use, how many shapes, what is common to all bricks.

time_bands.activity: Distribute wooden blocks (or unit cubes). Children handle the blocks freely, noting whether faces are flat or curved. Pose the prompt: 'Which building could you build with just these shapes?'

Try to make a model Q1–Q5 + Discussion, p.1 ("Make a model of buildings using blocks; answer: what parts..."). Children build, then pair-share answers to each discussion question — parts visible, shapes chosen, what changes if one block is removed.

Project Work, p.2 ("Observe a Qutub Minar model; answer what shape to use..."). Children examine the picture, discuss the shapes used for each section of the minar, and name what is common to all brick-shaped blocks.

periods.teacher_notes: Keep the block handling open and exploratory — resist naming shapes too early; let children produce their own words first. A common early error is calling any tall block a 'cylinder', regardless of whether its faces are flat or curved; prompt children to run a finger across each face to distinguish. Consolidation of shape vocabulary grows naturally from the building conversation.
materials: Wooden building blocks or unit cubes (enough for pairs)
Picture or small model of India Gate
Picture or small model of Qutub Minar

periods.activity_title: Folding Nets to Build Prisms and Pyramids

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Craft Q1, p.3
tasks_in_class.description: Make a sphere-like shape with paper strips.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Craft Q2, p.3
tasks_in_class.description: Use nets from the end of the book to make models of prisms (triangular, square, hexagonal) and pyramids (triangular, square, pentagonal); identify common face shapes and meeting points.

time_bands.activity: Craft Q1, p.3 ("Make a sphere-like shape with paper strips."). Children cut and weave paper strips into a globe-like form; observe that no flat net can make a perfect sphere.

Craft Q2, p.3 ("Use nets from the end of the book to make models of prisms..."). Children cut, fold, and glue nets to form at least one prism and one pyramid, then place models side by side. Class discusses: which faces are the same across all prisms? Where do the triangular faces of a pyramid meet?
Quick gallery walk: each group displays their models and names the shape. Class agrees on one sentence that tells what all pyramids have in common and one for all prisms.

periods.teacher_notes: Pre-score the fold lines on nets lightly with a dry ballpoint to help children fold cleanly without tearing. A frequent error is confusing a triangular prism with a triangular pyramid — guide children to count the triangular faces: two in a prism, all faces triangular only in a tetrahedron. Naming the meeting-point of triangular faces as the 'apex' may emerge naturally from discussion.
materials: Pre-printed nets from the textbook's cut-out pages (one set per pair)

periods.activity_title: Counting Faces, Edges, Corners — Finding the Pattern

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Craft Q3, p.4
tasks_in_class.description: Make shapes using straws and plasticine; fill in table of faces (F), corners (V), edges (E); identify F+V–E relationship.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Craft Q3 (sort by flat faces), p.4
tasks_in_class.description: Sort 3D shapes by number of flat faces and write names; determine if a 3D shape with 3 flat faces is possible.

homework.description: Sort 3D shapes by number of straight edges (6, 8, 9, 12) and write names.

time_bands.activity: Craft Q3, p.4 ("Make shapes using straws and plasticine; fill in table of faces (F), corners (V), edges (E)..."). Children build a cube, triangular prism, and square pyramid with straws and plasticine balls, then count and record F, V, E for each in the table. Each group then computes F + V − E and compares results across shapes.

Craft Q3 (sort by flat faces), p.4 ("Sort 3D shapes by number of flat faces and write names..."). Children arrange their models and the folded net-shapes from the building activity on the desk, sorted by face count. Class debates whether any 3D shape with exactly 3 flat faces could exist, using the models as evidence.

periods.teacher_notes: Children often miscount edges by tracing the same edge twice; suggest they mark each edge with a dot of chalk or a small sticker as they count. When the F + V − E values all turn out equal, celebrate the discovery before attaching a name to it — letting children articulate the pattern in their own words deepens retention. The homework sorting task directly extends the flat-face sorting done in class.
materials: Stickers or chalk for marking edges

section_titles: Faces, Edges, Corners — Observation and Classification
periods.activity_title: Reading a Die — Opposite Faces and Edge Neighbours

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Observe Q1, p.5
tasks_in_class.description: Take a die; identify the face opposite to faces numbered 2, 3, and 4.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Observe Q2, p.5
tasks_in_class.description: Identify which faces share edges with face 1, and which face has no common edge with face 1.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Observe Q3, p.5
tasks_in_class.description: Look at three views of the same cube; deduce the colour of the face opposite to red, and opposite to yellow.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Observe (border activity), p.5
tasks_in_class.description: Follow 5 instructions: colour rectangular-faced shapes red, add smileys to triangular-faced shapes, stars to curved-faced shapes, blue to shapes with no corner, circle shapes with same opposite faces.

time_bands.activity: Let Us Observe Q1, p.5 ("Take a die; identify the face opposite to faces numbered 2, 3, and 4.") and Let Us Observe Q2, p.5 ("Identify which faces share edges with face 1..."). Children handle a die and rotate it, recording opposite faces and edge-sharing faces in their books.

Let Us Observe Q3, p.5 ("Look at three views of the same cube; deduce the colour of the face opposite to red..."). Children study the three cube drawings, discuss in pairs, then write their deductions.

Let Us Observe (border activity), p.5 ("Follow 5 instructions: colour rectangular-faced shapes red..."). Children work through the five colouring and marking instructions independently, then compare with a partner.

periods.teacher_notes: Children frequently assume 'opposite faces' means adjacent faces; a physical die handled and slowly rotated resolves this quickly. For Q3, encourage children to note which colours they can see in each view before attempting to deduce the unseen face. The border activity consolidates face-type vocabulary built during net-making — connecting face shape to the name of the 3D solid strengthens both.
materials: One die per pair (or a cube model)

section_titles: Faces, Edges, Corners — Observation and Classification

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Sorting 3D Shapes Q1–Q3, p.6–7
tasks_in_class.description: Write names of 3D shapes in Venn-diagram circles sorted by: all faces same vs. not same; straight vs. curved edges; triangular vs. rectangular faces (with both-category).

time_bands.activity: Display or draw a simple two-circle Venn diagram on the board. Discuss what the overlapping region means, using a familiar non-maths example (animals that can swim AND fly). Children check their understanding before applying to shapes.

Sorting 3D Shapes Q1–Q3, p.6–7 ("Write names of 3D shapes in Venn-diagram circles sorted by: all faces same vs. not same..."). Children complete all three Venn diagrams. After each, a brief class share confirms placements and discusses any shape that sits in the overlapping region.

periods.teacher_notes: Children often place the sphere outside both circles of the straight/curved-edge diagram rather than in the 'curved edges only' region; prompt them to check whether a sphere has any straight edges. The three-sorting sequence (face sameness, edge type, face shape) recaps face and edge vocabulary from the net-making and straw-building activities — naming those ideas explicitly grounds the Venn work in what children have already handled. Watch for children placing a cylinder in the 'triangular faces' region by confusing circular and triangular.
materials: 3D shape models or pictures for reference (cube, cuboid, cylinder, cone, sphere, prisms, pyramids)

section_titles: Identifying 3D Shapes by Properties and Nets
periods.activity_title: Cube Towers, Dot-Paper Drawing, and Net Matching

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Build with Cubes A–D, p.7
tasks_in_class.description: Build models A, B, C, D with cubes from Jaadui Pitara Kit; count the cubes in each cube tower.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Drawing Cubes on a Triangular Dot Paper, p.8
tasks_in_class.description: Complete the partially drawn cubes on triangular dot paper.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Match the pictures Q1, p.8
tasks_in_class.description: Match six property-descriptions (faces, corners, edges) to the correct 3D shape names (a–f).

time_bands.activity: Build with Cubes A–D, p.7 ("Build models A, B, C, D with cubes from Jaadui Pitara Kit; count the cubes..."). Children build each model and count carefully, noting that hidden interior cubes must still be counted.

Drawing Cubes on a Triangular Dot Paper, p.8 ("Complete the partially drawn cubes on triangular dot paper."). Children follow the dots to extend the incomplete cube drawings; the teacher demonstrates one example on the board.

Match the pictures Q1, p.8 ("Match six property-descriptions (faces, corners, edges) to the correct 3D shape names..."). Children read each description, recall the counts from earlier building and net activities, and draw matching lines.

periods.teacher_notes: Children frequently undercount cubes in a tower by forgetting those hidden from view; encourage them to rotate the model or count layer by layer. On dot paper, the common error is drawing the back edges as visible — remind children that dashed lines show hidden edges. For the matching task, children who struggle may benefit from handling actual models while reading the property descriptions.
materials: Unit cubes from Jaadui Pitara Kit (or substitute cubes)
Triangular dot paper (textbook p.8 or printed sheet)

section_titles: Identifying 3D Shapes by Properties and Nets
periods.activity_title: How Are They Different? Nets, Folding, and Pieces

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Each one is different Q2, p.8
tasks_in_class.description: Discuss how a set of similar-looking shapes are each different from one another.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Match the nets Q3, p.9
tasks_in_class.description: Match four nets (1–4) to the appropriate solids (a–d).

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Which net Q4, p.9
tasks_in_class.description: Identify which of nets A, B, C, D can be folded to make the given solid.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Pieces of net Q5, p.9
tasks_in_class.description: Identify which solid (a–d) has the given pieces as parts of its net.

time_bands.activity: Each one is different Q2, p.8 ("Discuss how a set of similar-looking shapes are each different from one another."). Children examine the page, then talk in pairs before sharing with the class — naming one property that distinguishes each pair.
Match the nets Q3, p.9 ("Match four nets (1–4) to the appropriate solids (a–d)."). Children count faces in each net and compare to the solid's face count; draw matching lines.

Which net Q4, p.9 ("Identify which of nets A, B, C, D can be folded to make the given solid."). Children mentally (or physically, by tracing and cutting) test each net, eliminating those with wrong face shapes or count.
Pieces of net Q5, p.9 ("Identify which solid (a–d) has the given pieces as parts of its net."). Children assemble the partial pieces in their minds and identify the matching solid.

periods.teacher_notes: Children often match nets by shape of the largest face alone, ignoring the total face count; encourage them to count all faces in the net before deciding. For Q4, having a folded net model nearby helps children test their mental folding. A frequent misconception in Q5 is identifying the shape by a single distinctive face piece rather than checking that all pieces fit the same solid.
materials: Spare net cut-outs (optional, for physical folding check)

periods.activity_title: Making Angles with Straws and Folding the Right Angle

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do Q1 (mark angles), p.10
tasks_in_class.description: Mark angles in five pictures (scissors, book corner, clock hands, etc.).

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do Q2 (classroom angles), p.11
tasks_in_class.description: Give a few examples of where angles are seen in the classroom.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Right Angles (fold paper), p.11
tasks_in_class.description: Make a right angle with paper-folding; identify right angles in dot grid using a right-angle checker; find right angles in book, window, other objects.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do Q1 (draw right angles), p.12
tasks_in_class.description: Draw some right angles on the dot grid.

time_bands.activity: Let Us Do Q1 (mark angles), p.10 ("Mark angles in five pictures (scissors, book corner, clock hands, etc.)."). Children examine each picture and mark each visible angle with a small arc.

Let Us Do Q2 (classroom angles), p.11 ("Give a few examples of where angles are seen in the classroom."). Children look around the room and call out examples; the teacher lists them on the board and asks children to say where the two arms of each angle are.

Right Angles (fold paper), p.11 ("Make a right angle with paper-folding; identify right angles in dot grid..."). Each child folds paper twice to make a right-angle checker, then uses it to test corners on textbooks, windows, and table edges before marking right angles in the dot grid.
Let Us Do Q1 (draw right angles), p.12 ("Draw some right angles on the dot grid."). Children use the dot grid to draw several right angles, checking each with their paper folder.

periods.teacher_notes: Children sometimes mark the interior region of a shape rather than the angle itself; demonstrate marking the small arc at the meeting point of two arms. The paper-fold right-angle checker is central to this unit — ensure every child makes one before moving to testing and drawing. A common error when drawing on dot grids is making one arm diagonal, which the checker will immediately reveal as not a right angle.
materials: Two straws per child (for angle-making demonstration)
Plain paper for folding (one sheet per child)
Dot-grid paper (textbook p.12 or printed sheet)

periods.activity_title: Naming and Drawing Acute and Obtuse Angles

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Acute and Obtuse Angles (naming objects), p.12
tasks_in_class.description: Name classroom objects that have an acute angle; name objects that have an obtuse angle.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Acute and Obtuse Angles (letters), p.12
tasks_in_class.description: Identify all angles in the given letter shapes.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do Q1 (draw acute/obtuse), p.13
tasks_in_class.description: Draw some acute angles on the top grid; draw a line to make an acute angle using each given line in the bottom grid. Repeat for obtuse angles.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do Q2 (colour-code angles), p.13
tasks_in_class.description: Mark acute angles in red, right angles in green, and obtuse angles in blue in given figures.

time_bands.activity: Acute and Obtuse Angles (naming objects), p.12 ("Name classroom objects that have an acute angle; name objects that have an obtuse angle."). Children compare each object's angle to their paper right-angle checker from the right-angles activity: smaller than the checker = acute, larger = obtuse.
Acute and Obtuse Angles (letters), p.12 ("Identify all angles in the given letter shapes."). Children label each angle in the letters as A (acute), R (right), or O (obtuse).

Let Us Do Q1 (draw acute/obtuse), p.13 ("Draw some acute angles on the top grid; draw a line to make an acute angle using each given line..."). Children draw, then check each angle with their paper folder before completing the obtuse-angle section.
Let Us Do Q2 (colour-code angles), p.13 ("Mark acute angles in red, right angles in green, and obtuse angles in blue in given figures."). Children colour each angle arc with the appropriate colour.

periods.teacher_notes: Children frequently confuse acute and obtuse because they focus on the shape of the figure rather than the angle size; anchoring every classification to the right-angle checker comparison is the most reliable correction. The paper-fold right-angle checker used in the right-angles work functions as the standard throughout this unit — having children keep it on their desks avoids guessing. A persistent error in letter-angle tasks is missing angles formed inside concave letter shapes like 'E' or 'F'.
materials: Paper right-angle checkers (each child makes or brings from right-angles work)

section_titles: Shapes with Straws — Rigidity and 2D Shapes

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Shapes with Straws (triangle and rectangle), p.14
tasks_in_class.description: Make triangle and rectangle with straws and clay; push sides; trace shapes; observe rigidity and angle changes. Repeat for square and pentagon.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Shapes with Straws (pentagon and circle), p.16
tasks_in_class.description: Make a pentagon with equal straws; push a side and observe angle change. Investigate whether a circle can be made with straws; observe what happens with unequal straws.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: 4-sided shapes, p.15
tasks_in_class.description: Examine given 4-sided shapes; discuss in what ways rectangle and square differ from the other shapes shown.

homework.description: Draw several three- and four-sided shapes on the dot grid; circle shapes with one or more right angles; count shapes with 1, 2, 3, all right angles.

time_bands.activity: Shapes with Straws (triangle and rectangle), p.14 ("Make triangle and rectangle with straws and clay; push sides; trace shapes; observe rigidity and angle changes. Repeat for square and pentagon."). Children build, push, and trace in sequence, writing one observation about each shape's behaviour when pushed.

Shapes with Straws (pentagon and circle), p.16 ("Make a pentagon with equal straws; push a side and observe angle change. Investigate whether a circle can be made with straws..."). Children test equal and unequal straws, then discuss why a circle cannot be made.

4-sided shapes, p.15 ("Examine given 4-sided shapes; discuss in what ways rectangle and square differ from the other shapes shown."). Children study the figures and articulate at least two properties that set rectangles and squares apart.

periods.teacher_notes: The key discovery — that triangles are rigid while quadrilaterals are not — should come from children's own pushing and tracing rather than being stated first. A common misconception is that a square pushed at one corner remains a square; tracing before and after shows the angles have changed. Connecting the right-angle property of rectangles and squares to the paper-checker work on acute, right, and obtuse angles gives children a property-based rather than appearance-based definition.
materials: Straws cut to at least three different lengths
Plasticine or clay balls for joints

periods.activity_title: Paper-Folding the Circle — Discovering Radius and Diameter

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Make (draw circle with scale), p.16
tasks_in_class.description: Mark a point A; draw many points equidistant from A; connect dots freehand to get a circle. Identify centre and radius.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Amazing Circles Q1–Q5, p.17
tasks_in_class.description: Fold circular paper in half three different ways; measure each crease; note all creases are equal (diameters); measure radius; discuss relationship between radius and diameter.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do (diameter fold), p.18
tasks_in_class.description: Fold circular paper in half then half again to find that diameter is double the radius.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Look at the wheels, p.19
tasks_in_class.description: Observe wheels A, B, C, D; name the wheel with longest radius, shortest radius, longest diameter, shortest diameter.

homework.description: Use a compass (with teacher help) to draw the three-step circle design; mark centre, radius, and diameter on the carpet design.

time_bands.activity: Let Us Make (draw circle with scale), p.16 ("Mark a point A; draw many points equidistant from A; connect dots freehand to get a circle."). Children use a ruler to mark eight or more points at the same distance from A, then join them. They label the centre and draw one radius.

Amazing Circles Q1–Q5, p.17 ("Fold circular paper in half three different ways; measure each crease..."). Children fold circular cut-outs three times in different directions, measure each crease with a thread or strip of paper, and record whether they are equal. Class shares findings before naming the crease as 'diameter'.

Let Us Do (diameter fold), p.18 ("Fold circular paper in half then half again to find that diameter is double the radius."). Children fold and measure to confirm the relationship, then write it in their own words.
Look at the wheels, p.19 ("Observe wheels A, B, C, D; name the wheel with longest radius..."). Children compare the four wheels and use the diameter = 2 × radius relationship to answer.

periods.teacher_notes: The equidistant-points construction in the opening task grounds the definition of a circle physically before the word 'radius' is introduced — let children articulate that all their lines from the centre are equal before you supply the term. A frequent error in the folding activity is measuring the fold line from edge to fold rather than across the full diameter; demonstrate how to open the paper flat and measure the full crease. The compass design homework requires adult supervision; alert children to ask a family member for help.
materials: Circular paper cut-outs (one per child, at least 3 for folding)
Thread or paper strips for measuring creases

section_titles: Let Us Try — Reasoning and Puzzle Tasks
periods.activity_title: Hidden Shapes, Sorting Cards, and Matchstick Puzzles

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Puzzling Shapes Q1–Q4, p.19–20
tasks_in_class.description: Identify hidden shapes and write names; draw 2 lines to divide triangle into 1 square + 2 triangles; draw 2 lines to divide square into 3 triangles; draw cuts on shapes to get specified smaller shapes.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Card Game, p.20
tasks_in_class.description: Sort 2D-shape cards into three groups by number of sides; draw sorted shapes and explain sorting.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Try Q1 (Squiggly spiders), p.21
tasks_in_class.description: Count triangles in triangular web; trace a path from A back to A without reusing a wall. Count rectangles in rectangular web; trace a path from A to B without reusing a wall.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Try Q2 (matchsticks — 2 triangles), p.21
tasks_in_class.description: Use 5 matchsticks to make 2 triangles; draw it.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Try Q6 (classify by angles), p.22
tasks_in_class.description: Classify shapes a–g into 3 angles / 4 angles / 5 angles groups; identify the relation between number of sides and number of angles.

time_bands.activity: Puzzling Shapes Q1–Q4, p.19–20 ("Identify hidden shapes and write names; draw 2 lines to divide triangle into 1 square + 2 triangles..."). Children work through each sub-task, drawing lines carefully and naming each resulting shape.
Card Game, p.20 ("Sort 2D-shape cards into three groups by number of sides..."). Children sort, draw, and write a one-sentence explanation of their grouping criterion.

Let Us Try Q1 (Squiggly spiders), p.21 ("Count triangles in triangular web; trace a path from A back to A..."). Children count first, then attempt the path tracing, marking paths with a pencil. Compare attempts with a partner.

Let Us Try Q2 (matchsticks — 2 triangles), p.21 ("Use 5 matchsticks to make 2 triangles; draw it."). Children experiment with actual matchsticks or drawn lines, discovering that sharing one side allows 2 triangles with only 5 sticks.

Let Us Try Q6 (classify by angles), p.22 ("Classify shapes a–g into 3 angles / 4 angles / 5 angles groups; identify the relation between number of sides and number of angles."). Children complete the classification then articulate the sides-equal-angles pattern.

periods.teacher_notes: Children tackling the hidden-shapes puzzles often miss shapes that are formed across the whole figure, not just single cells; suggest they outline each candidate shape with a different colour. For the spider-web path tracing, many children try to retrace a wall rather than accepting that no perfect circuit is possible in the rectangular web — this difficulty is itself the discovery. The sides-equal-angles observation in Q6 sets up a pattern that the synthesis unit revisits across all polygon types.
materials: 2D shape cards (cut from textbook end-pages or pre-made cards)
Matchsticks (5 per child) or short sticks

section_titles: Faces, Edges, Corners — Observation and Classification
Identifying 3D Shapes by Properties and Nets
Shapes with Straws — Rigidity and 2D Shapes
Let Us Try — Reasoning and Puzzle Tasks
periods.activity_title: Shapes Around Us — A Chapter-Wide Challenge Trail

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Try Q3 (move 2 matchsticks — 4 triangles), p.22
tasks_in_class.description: Move two matchsticks from the given arrangement to form 4 triangles.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Try Q4 (remove 4 matchsticks — 3 triangles), p.22
tasks_in_class.description: Remove 4 matchsticks from the given arrangement to leave only 3 triangles.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Try Q5 (model challenge), p.22
tasks_in_class.description: Make solid shape models using: (a) 12 straws + 8 clay balls; (b) 9 straws + 6 clay balls; (c) 15 straws + 10 clay balls; (d) 10 straws + 6 clay balls.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Try Q7 (draw 2D shapes), p.23
tasks_in_class.description: Draw a 2D shape with fewer than 5 angles; draw a 2D shape with more than 5 angles.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Try Q8 (mark right angles), p.23
tasks_in_class.description: Mark right angles in each figure; write the number of right angles; identify shapes with only right angles.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Try Q9 (identify angle types in shapes), p.23
tasks_in_class.description: Identify the shape that has: 2 right + 1 acute + 1 obtuse; 1 right + 2 obtuse + 1 acute; 2 obtuse + 2 acute; 4 right angles.

time_bands.activity: Let Us Try Q3, p.22 ("Move two matchsticks from the given arrangement to form 4 triangles.") and Let Us Try Q4, p.22 ("Remove 4 matchsticks from the given arrangement to leave only 3 triangles."). Children work individually then share solutions, drawing the before-and-after arrangements. The teacher connects these to all the triangle properties explored across the chapter.

Let Us Try Q5 (model challenge), p.22 ("Make solid shape models using: (a) 12 straws + 8 clay balls; (b) 9 straws + 6 clay balls..."). Children use the E (straws) and V (clay balls) counts together with the F + V − E relationship and their knowledge of prisms and pyramids to identify and build each solid. Groups compare and confirm.

Let Us Try Q7, p.23 ("Draw a 2D shape with fewer than 5 angles; draw a 2D shape with more than 5 angles.") and Let Us Try Q8, p.23 ("Mark right angles in each figure; write the number of right angles..."). Children draw, mark, and count, then use the sides-equal-angles pattern to predict angle counts before drawing.

Let Us Try Q9, p.23 ("Identify the shape that has: 2 right + 1 acute + 1 obtuse..."). Children match each angle combination to a shape, using the angle vocabulary built across the chapter. A brief whole-class discussion closes the unit: 'What one shape could you not build without everything we know about faces, angles, and properties?'

periods.teacher_notes: The model challenge draws directly on the F + V − E relationship discovered during straw-and-plasticine building: children who use E = straws and V = clay balls to compute F can narrow down the shape quickly. The closing discussion question — asking children to name one shape that required multiple chapter ideas — surfaces the connections between 3D structure, nets, angle types, and 2D properties that run through the whole chapter. Watch for children who mark a right angle on a diagonal shape as acute; the paper-fold checker from angle work is still the best correction tool.
materials: Straws and clay balls (for model challenge)

tasks.book_ref: Craft Q2, p.3
tasks.description: Use nets from the end of the book to make models of prisms (triangular, square, hexagonal) and pyramids (triangular, square, pentagonal); identify common face shapes and meeting points.

tasks.book_ref: Build with Cubes A–D, p.7
tasks.description: Build models A, B, C, D with cubes from Jaadui Pitara Kit; count the cubes in each cube tower.

tasks.book_ref: Right Angles (fold paper), p.11
tasks.description: Make a right angle with paper-folding; identify right angles in dot grid using a right-angle checker; find right angles in book, window, other objects.

tasks.book_ref: Shapes with Straws (triangle and rectangle), p.14
tasks.description: Make triangle and rectangle with straws and clay; push sides; trace shapes; observe rigidity and angle changes. Repeat for square and pentagon.

tasks.book_ref: Let Us Make (draw circle with scale), p.16
tasks.description: Mark a point A; draw many points equidistant from A; connect dots freehand to get a circle. Identify centre and radius.

tasks.book_ref: Amazing Circles Q1–Q5, p.17
tasks.description: Fold circular paper in half three different ways; measure each crease; note all creases are equal (diameters); measure radius; discuss relationship between radius and diameter.

tasks.book_ref: Let Us Try Q2 (matchsticks — 2 triangles), p.21
tasks.description: Use 5 matchsticks to make 2 triangles; draw it.

tasks.book_ref: Craft Q3, p.4
tasks.description: Make shapes using straws and plasticine; fill in table of faces (F), corners (V), edges (E); identify F+V–E relationship.

tasks.book_ref: Craft Q3 (sort by flat faces), p.4
tasks.description: Sort 3D shapes by number of flat faces and write names; determine if a 3D shape with 3 flat faces is possible.

tasks.book_ref: Let Us Observe Q3, p.5
tasks.description: Look at three views of the same cube; deduce the colour of the face opposite to red, and opposite to yellow.

tasks.book_ref: Sorting 3D Shapes Q1–Q3, p.6–7

items.section_title: 3D Shapes — Modelling and Exploring
items.prompt: Look at a brick. It has flat faces and straight edges. Name the 3D shape that a brick is, and say how many flat faces it has.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A brick is a cuboid. It has 6 flat faces.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the shape by its flat rectangular faces and count them.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student handle a real brick or box and count faces by touching; stretch: ask them to name one building part that looks like each 3D shape.

exercise.book_ref: Try to make a model Q1–Q5 + Discussion, p.1
exercise.description: Make a model of buildings using blocks; answer: what parts shown, why selected, what shapes, how similar/different, what if one piece removed.

items.section_title: Nets, Prisms, and Pyramids
items.prompt: A shape is made by folding a net. The net has 2 triangles and 3 rectangles. What solid does it make?

options.label: A
options.text: Cuboid

options.label: B
options.text: Square pyramid

options.label: C
options.text: Triangular prism

options.label: D
options.text: Triangular pyramid

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Triangular prism — it has 2 triangular faces and 3 rectangular faces.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count and identify face shapes in the net to name the solid.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student knows pyramids have triangular faces but does not distinguish prisms from pyramids.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student counts 5 faces correctly but does not attend to face shape — cuboid has 6 rectangular faces.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student conflates triangular prism with triangular pyramid; both have triangular faces but the net face count differs.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student fold a spare net and hold the model; stretch: ask them to draw what the net of a square prism would look like.

exercise.book_ref: Craft Q2, p.3
exercise.description: Use nets from the end of the book to make models of prisms (triangular, square, hexagonal) and pyramids (triangular, square, pentagonal); identify common face shapes and meeting points.

items.section_title: Building and Drawing with Cubes
items.prompt: A tower is built by stacking cubes in layers: 3 cubes in the bottom layer, 2 cubes in the middle layer, and 1 cube on top. How many cubes are in the tower altogether?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 6 cubes.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count cubes layer by layer and add: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student build the tower with real cubes and count; stretch: ask how many cubes would be needed for one more layer of 4 at the bottom.

exercise.book_ref: Build with Cubes A–D, p.7
exercise.description: Build models A, B, C, D with cubes from Jaadui Pitara Kit; count the cubes in each cube tower.

items.section_title: Angles — Introduction and Right Angles
items.prompt: Fold a piece of paper twice to make a right-angle checker. Use it to check the corner of your textbook. Is the corner a right angle? How do you know?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes, the corner is a right angle. The folded paper fits exactly on the corner — neither arm sticks out nor leaves a gap.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Place the paper-fold right-angle checker against the corner and observe whether the edges align exactly.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: guide the student to hold the checker firmly in the corner and look for gaps; stretch: ask them to find one object in the room whose corner is NOT a right angle and explain why.

exercise.book_ref: Right Angles (fold paper), p.11
exercise.description: Make a right angle with paper-folding; identify right angles in dot grid using a right-angle checker; find right angles in book, window, other objects.

items.section_title: Shapes with Straws — Rigidity and 2D Shapes
items.prompt: Riya makes a triangle and a rectangle with straws and clay. She pushes one side of each shape. What does she observe?

options.label: A
options.text: Both shapes change their angles when pushed.

options.label: B
options.text: Neither shape changes when pushed.

options.label: C
options.text: The rectangle keeps its shape; the triangle changes shape.

options.label: D
options.text: The triangle keeps its shape; the rectangle changes shape.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The triangle keeps its shape; the rectangle changes shape.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Push a straw side — the triangle is rigid because its angles are fixed by its three sides; the rectangle's angles can change.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student has not made or tested the shapes and guesses that all shapes deform.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student has the correct idea about rigidity but has swapped which shape is rigid.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student believes all shapes made with stiff straws stay fixed, ignoring that the clay joints allow rotation.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student make both shapes with straws and clay and push them physically; stretch: ask whether a pentagon would be rigid or flexible and why.

exercise.book_ref: Shapes with Straws (triangle and rectangle), p.14
exercise.description: Make triangle and rectangle with straws and clay; push sides; trace shapes; observe rigidity and angle changes. Repeat for square and pentagon.

items.section_title: Circles — Radius and Diameter
items.prompt: Priya folds a circular piece of paper in half three different ways and measures each crease with a thread. What does she find about the lengths of the creases?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: All three creases are equal in length. Each crease is a diameter and passes through the centre of the circle.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fold the circle in different directions and compare crease lengths — they are all equal because each is a diameter.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student fold and measure just one crease, then compare with a partner's crease; stretch: ask what would happen to the crease length if the circle were bigger.

exercise.book_ref: Amazing Circles Q1–Q5, p.17
exercise.description: Fold circular paper in half three different ways; measure each crease; note all creases are equal (diameters); measure radius; discuss relationship between radius and diameter.

items.section_title: Let Us Try — Reasoning and Puzzle Tasks
items.prompt: Use 5 matchsticks to make exactly 2 triangles. Draw your arrangement. How many matchsticks does each triangle share with the other?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Place 3 matchsticks to form one triangle, then use 2 of those sides plus 1 new matchstick to form a second triangle sharing one side. Each triangle shares 1 matchstick with the other.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Two triangles sharing one side need 3 + 3 − 1 = 5 matchsticks.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student real matchsticks to move physically before drawing; stretch: ask if 7 matchsticks could make 3 triangles, and how.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Try Q2 (matchsticks — 2 triangles), p.21
exercise.description: Use 5 matchsticks to make 2 triangles; draw it.

items.section_title: Nets, Prisms, and Pyramids
items.prompt: A cuboid has 6 faces, 8 corners, and 12 edges. A triangular prism has 5 faces, 6 corners, and 9 edges. Work out F + V − E for each shape. What do you notice?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Cuboid: 6 + 8 − 12 = 2. Triangular prism: 5 + 6 − 9 = 2. The result is 2 for both shapes.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Substitute F, V, E values and compute; compare results across shapes.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write the formula F + V − E = ? on the board and guide the student to substitute one value at a time; stretch: ask them to predict F + V − E for a square pyramid (5 faces, 5 corners, 8 edges) before computing.

exercise.book_ref: Craft Q3, p.4
exercise.description: Make shapes using straws and plasticine; fill in table of faces (F), corners (V), edges (E); identify F+V–E relationship.

items.section_title: Nets, Prisms, and Pyramids
items.prompt: Shapes are sorted by number of flat faces. Which group is correct?
items.visual_stimulus:
| Number of flat faces | Shape name |
| 0 | Sphere |
| 2 | Cylinder |
| 5 | Square pyramid |

options.label: A
options.text: Sphere: 0 flat faces; Cylinder: 2 flat faces; Square pyramid: 4 flat faces

options.label: B
options.text: Sphere: 0 flat faces; Cylinder: 2 flat faces; Square pyramid: 5 flat faces

options.label: C
options.text: Sphere: 0 flat faces; Cylinder: 3 flat faces; Square pyramid: 5 flat faces

options.label: D
options.text: Sphere: 1 flat face; Cylinder: 2 flat faces; Square pyramid: 5 flat faces

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Sphere: 0, Cylinder: 2, Square pyramid: 5.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify each face as flat or curved and count only the flat ones.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Student counts the curved surface of a sphere as a flat face.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student counts the curved surface of a cylinder as a third face alongside the two circular ends.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student counts only the four triangular faces of a square pyramid and forgets the square base.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student run a finger over each face of a model and say 'flat' or 'curved'; stretch: ask how many flat faces a triangular pyramid has.

exercise.book_ref: Craft Q3 (sort by flat faces), p.4
exercise.description: Sort 3D shapes by number of flat faces and write names; determine if a 3D shape with 3 flat faces is possible.

items.section_title: Faces, Edges, Corners — Observation and Classification
items.prompt: Three views of the same cube are shown. In view 1, the top face is red and the front face is blue. In view 2, the top face is blue and the front face is green. What colour is the face opposite to red?

options.label: A
options.text: Blue

options.label: B
options.text: Green

options.label: C
options.text: Red

options.label: D
options.text: Yellow

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Green. In view 1 red is on top; in view 2 blue has moved to the top, so red has moved to the bottom. In view 2 the front is green, which is adjacent to blue (top) — but since red is now the bottom face, the face opposite to red is the original top position when the cube is in view 2 orientation, which is green.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Track the position of the red face across views to determine which face is directly opposite it.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student thinks the face adjacent to red in view 1 (blue) must be opposite it.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student does not understand that a face cannot be opposite itself.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student guesses a colour not established in the given views.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student mark a real cube's faces with coloured stickers and rotate it to match each view; stretch: ask them to deduce a fourth colour's position if yellow appears on the right in view 1.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Observe Q3, p.5
exercise.description: Look at three views of the same cube; deduce the colour of the face opposite to red, and opposite to yellow.

items.section_title: Faces, Edges, Corners — Observation and Classification
items.prompt: A cylinder and a cone are placed in the group 'has at least one curved edge.' A cube and a cuboid are placed in the group 'all edges are straight.' Which shape could go into BOTH groups? Give a reason.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: No shape from the standard set can go into both groups because a shape either has curved edges or it does not. A cone or cylinder has curved edges only (no straight edges), and a cube or cuboid has straight edges only (no curved edges). No shape belongs to both.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check each shape: does it have both curved and straight edges? Cube/cuboid — no curved edges. Cylinder/cone — no straight edges.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student a cylinder and a cube to handle and count each type of edge; stretch: ask whether any 3D shape in the chapter has BOTH straight and curved edges, and to justify their answer.

exercise.book_ref: Sorting 3D Shapes Q1–Q3, p.6–7
exercise.description: Write names of 3D shapes in Venn-diagram circles sorted by: all faces same vs. not same; straight vs. curved edges; triangular vs. rectangular faces (with both-category).

items.section_title: Identifying 3D Shapes by Properties and Nets
items.prompt: A 3D shape has 6 faces, 8 corners, and 12 edges. All its faces are rectangles. What is the shape?

options.label: A
options.text: Cube

options.label: B
options.text: Cuboid

options.label: C
options.text: Hexagonal prism

options.label: D
options.text: Square prism only if all faces are squares

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Cuboid — 6 rectangular faces, 8 corners, 12 edges.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Match the face shape and count (6 rectangular faces, 8 corners, 12 edges) to the shape name.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student knows a cube has 6 faces and 8 corners but does not notice that a cube's faces are squares (a special rectangle), so the clue 'all rectangles' also fits a cube — however, the intended answer is the general case (cuboid). Accept cube with justification.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student introduces unnecessary qualification not needed to identify the shape.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student does not check the face count — a hexagonal prism has 8 faces.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student check each property against a cuboid model; stretch: ask them to write the F, V, E values for a triangular prism and verify F + V − E.

exercise.book_ref: Match the pictures Q1, p.8
exercise.description: Match six property-descriptions (faces, corners, edges) to the correct 3D shape names (a–f).

items.section_title: Identifying 3D Shapes by Properties and Nets
items.prompt: Which net has exactly 4 triangles and 1 square, and folds into a pyramid?

options.label: A
options.text: A net with 1 rectangle and 4 triangles

options.label: B
options.text: A net with 1 square in the centre and 4 triangles attached to each side of the square

options.label: C
options.text: A net with 2 triangles and 3 rectangles

options.label: D
options.text: A net with 6 squares

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A net with 1 square in the centre and 4 triangles attached to each side of the square — this folds into a square pyramid.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the faces in the net: 1 square base + 4 triangular faces = square pyramid.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Student identifies triangular faces but associates them with a prism rather than a pyramid.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student recognises 6 faces but ignores the face shape — 6 squares make a cube.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student counts 4 triangles correctly but replaces the square base with a rectangle, which would make a rectangular pyramid.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student count the faces in each net description and check against a folded net model; stretch: ask what solid the net with 1 rectangle and 4 triangles would form.

exercise.book_ref: Match the nets Q3, p.9
exercise.description: Match four nets (1–4) to the appropriate solids (a–d).

items.section_title: Identifying 3D Shapes by Properties and Nets
items.prompt: Net P has 2 large rectangles, 2 small rectangles, and 2 squares. Net Q has 4 identical rectangles and 2 squares. Can both nets fold into a cuboid? Explain your thinking.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Both nets have 6 faces in total, all rectangles (squares are special rectangles). Both can fold into a cuboid — Net P makes a cuboid with different-sized faces, and Net Q also makes a cuboid where two faces are square. Yes, both can fold into a cuboid.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count faces in each net (must be 6) and check that all faces are rectangles — both conditions for a cuboid.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to count total faces in each net first; stretch: ask whether the two cuboids would look identical or different, and why.

exercise.book_ref: Which net Q4, p.9
exercise.description: Identify which of nets A, B, C, D can be folded to make the given solid.

items.section_title: Angles — Introduction and Right Angles
items.prompt: Look around your classroom. Name two objects that show an angle. For each object, say where the two arms of the angle are.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Acceptable examples: open book (the two covers are the two arms; the spine is where they meet); open door (the wall and the door edge are the arms; the hinge is the vertex); clock hands (each hand is an arm; the centre is the vertex). Any two well-described examples accepted.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the two straight arms of an angle and the point where they meet in a real object.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to point to an angle rather than describe it first, then put it into words; stretch: ask whether the angle in their first example is acute, right, or obtuse.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do Q2 (classroom angles), p.11
exercise.description: Give a few examples of where angles are seen in the classroom.

items.section_title: Acute and Obtuse Angles
items.prompt: A student compares three angles to a right-angle checker. Angle P fits exactly inside the checker (smaller). Angle Q is exactly the same as the checker. Angle R is bigger than the checker. What types are P, Q, and R?

options.label: A
options.text: P is acute; Q is a right angle; R is obtuse

options.label: B
options.text: P is acute; Q is acute; R is obtuse

options.label: C
options.text: P is obtuse; Q is a right angle; R is acute

options.label: D
options.text: P is right; Q is acute; R is obtuse

teacher_guide.expected_answer: P is acute (smaller than a right angle), Q is a right angle (exactly matches the checker), R is obtuse (larger than a right angle).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare each angle to the right-angle checker: smaller = acute, equal = right angle, larger = obtuse.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Student has swapped acute and obtuse — thinks a smaller angle is obtuse.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student correctly identifies P as acute and R as obtuse but does not recognise Q as a distinct type (right angle).
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student confuses the angle that matches the checker with an acute angle.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student place a paper right-angle checker against drawn angles and describe what they see; stretch: ask them to draw one angle of each type on dot paper.

exercise.book_ref: Acute and Obtuse Angles (naming objects), p.12
exercise.description: Name classroom objects that have an acute angle; name objects that have an obtuse angle.

items.section_title: Shapes with Straws — Rigidity and 2D Shapes
items.prompt: Manu makes a pentagon with five equal straws. He pushes one side. Do the angles of the pentagon change? What does this tell you about a pentagon compared with a triangle?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes, the angles change when a side of the pentagon is pushed. This shows that a pentagon is not rigid — its angles can change. A triangle is rigid because pushing any side does not change its angles.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Test rigidity by pushing a side and observing whether angles change; compare triangle (rigid) to pentagon (not rigid).
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student make the pentagon and triangle with straws and clay and test physically; stretch: ask why a pentagon might be made rigid if a diagonal straw were added inside it.

exercise.book_ref: Shapes with Straws (pentagon and circle), p.16
exercise.description: Make a pentagon with equal straws; push a side and observe angle change. Investigate whether a circle can be made with straws; observe what happens with unequal straws.

items.section_title: Shapes with Straws — Rigidity and 2D Shapes
items.prompt: Look at two 4-sided shapes: a rectangle and a shape that looks like a slanted rectangle (a parallelogram with no right angles). Name one way they are the same and one way they are different.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Same: both have 4 sides. Different: the rectangle has 4 right angles; the slanted shape does not — it has 2 acute and 2 obtuse angles.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the number of sides (same) and angle types (different) of the two 4-sided shapes.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to use a right-angle checker on each shape and report what they find; stretch: ask whether both shapes could be pushed flat (i.e. which is rigid).

exercise.book_ref: 4-sided shapes, p.15
exercise.description: Examine given 4-sided shapes; discuss in what ways rectangle and square differ from the other shapes shown.

items.section_title: Circles — Radius and Diameter
items.prompt: Noor folds a circle in half. The crease is 10 cm long. What is the radius of the circle?

options.label: A
options.text: 2 cm

options.label: B
options.text: 5 cm

options.label: C
options.text: 10 cm

options.label: D
options.text: 20 cm

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 5 cm. The crease is the diameter (10 cm). Radius = diameter ÷ 2 = 5 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fold crease = diameter; radius = diameter ÷ 2.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Student confuses radius with diameter — gives the diameter as the radius.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student doubles the diameter instead of halving it.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student divides by 5 instead of 2, perhaps confusing the relationship.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a circle with the crease labelled and ask the student to fold it again in half to find the radius; stretch: ask what the diameter would be if the radius were 8 cm.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do (diameter fold), p.18
exercise.description: Fold circular paper in half then half again to find that diameter is double the radius.

items.section_title: Circles — Radius and Diameter
items.prompt: Four wheels are drawn. Wheel W has a radius of 6 cm. Wheel X has a radius of 4 cm. Wheel Y has a diameter of 14 cm. Wheel Z has a diameter of 8 cm. Which wheel has the longest diameter? Which has the shortest radius?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Wheel Y has the longest diameter (14 cm). Wheel X has the shortest radius (4 cm).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Convert all to the same measure (diameter = 2 × radius) and compare: W=12 cm, X=8 cm, Y=14 cm, Z=8 cm diameter.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to convert each wheel's radius to diameter (or vice versa) one at a time before comparing; stretch: ask them to order all four wheels from smallest to largest diameter.

exercise.book_ref: Look at the wheels, p.19
exercise.description: Observe wheels A, B, C, D; name the wheel with longest radius, shortest radius, longest diameter, shortest diameter.

items.section_title: Puzzling Shapes and 2D Shape Sorting
items.prompt: Draw a large triangle. Draw exactly 2 straight lines inside it to make 1 square and 2 triangles. Describe where you placed the two lines.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Draw a right-angled triangle. One line parallel to the base creates a smaller triangle at the top. A second line vertical from the base to the first line creates a square in the lower portion. The square sits at the right angle corner; the remaining two pieces are triangles.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Place one line to cut off a top triangle; place a second line perpendicular to the base to form a square from the right-angle corner.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student a pre-drawn large right-angled triangle and let them try multiple line placements with a pencil before committing; stretch: ask them to check that the quadrilateral they formed really has 4 right angles (using the checker).

exercise.book_ref: Puzzling Shapes Q1–Q4, p.19–20
exercise.description: Identify hidden shapes and write names; draw 2 lines to divide triangle into 1 square + 2 triangles; draw 2 lines to divide square into 3 triangles; draw cuts on shapes to get specified smaller shapes.

items.section_title: Let Us Try — Reasoning and Puzzle Tasks
items.prompt: A spider-web diagram has triangles inside it. Anu counts 6 small triangles. She also tries to trace a path from point A back to point A without reusing any wall. Can she do it? Give a reason.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes, she can trace a closed path from A back to A without reusing any wall in a triangular web, because every junction point (vertex) has an even number of walls meeting it, which is the condition for a closed Eulerian path.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check whether every vertex in the web has an even number of edges meeting it — if so, an Euler circuit exists.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw the web and trace with a pencil, crossing off each wall after use; stretch: ask whether the rectangular web allows a path from A back to A and why (it does not, because some vertices are odd-degree).

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Try Q1 (Squiggly spiders), p.21
exercise.description: Count triangles in triangular web; trace a path from A back to A without reusing a wall. Count rectangles in rectangular web; trace a path from A to B without reusing a wall.

items.section_title: Let Us Try — Reasoning and Puzzle Tasks
items.prompt: Some matchsticks are arranged to show 5 triangles. You move exactly 2 matchsticks. Draw the new arrangement that gives exactly 4 triangles.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: One valid solution: start with a row of 3 triangles sharing sides (5 matchsticks along the bottom, plus tops). Move 2 matchsticks from the outer triangle positions to create an inner arrangement giving 4 triangles — the exact drawing depends on the textbook figure, but 4 non-overlapping triangles must be visible after exactly 2 moves.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Systematically try moving each matchstick and count resulting triangles; stop when count reaches 4.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student real matchsticks and the starting arrangement drawn on paper to copy; stretch: ask how many matchsticks the minimum arrangement of 4 non-overlapping triangles would need.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Try Q3 (move 2 matchsticks — 4 triangles), p.22
exercise.description: Move two matchsticks from the given arrangement to form 4 triangles.

items.section_title: Let Us Try — Reasoning and Puzzle Tasks
items.prompt: Shape P has 5 sides. How many angles does it have?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 5 angles — a polygon has the same number of angles as sides.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the pattern: number of angles = number of sides in any polygon.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student subtracts 1, perhaps thinking the last side 'closes' the shape without creating a new angle.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student adds 1, perhaps thinking the closing side creates an extra angle.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student doubles the number of sides, perhaps confusing sides with the total number of endpoints.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a pentagon and point to each angle in turn while counting sides; stretch: ask how many angles a 7-sided shape has and challenge them to draw one.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Try Q6 (classify by angles), p.22
exercise.description: Classify shapes a–g into 3 angles / 4 angles / 5 angles groups; identify the relation between number of sides and number of angles.

items.section_title: Let Us Try — Reasoning and Puzzle Tasks
items.prompt: Which shape has exactly 2 right angles, 1 acute angle, and 1 obtuse angle?

options.label: A
options.text: A quadrilateral with two right-angle corners, one sharp corner, and one wide corner

options.label: B
options.text: A rectangle

options.label: C
options.text: A square

options.label: D
options.text: A triangle with one right angle and two acute angles

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A quadrilateral with 2 right angles, 1 acute, and 1 obtuse angle. This is a 4-angled shape with a specific mix of angle types.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the required number of angles (4 total) and match angle types: 2 right + 1 acute + 1 obtuse.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student identifies a quadrilateral but forgets that a rectangle has 4 right angles, not 2.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student counts angles correctly (3) but ignores the requirement for 2 right angles in a 4-angled shape.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student associates right angles with a square but a square has 4 right angles, not a mixed set.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to draw a 4-sided shape and mark its angles, then check against the description; stretch: ask them to draw the shape and mark each angle type with a different colour.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Try Q9 (identify angle types in shapes), p.23
exercise.description: Identify the shape that has: 2 right + 1 acute + 1 obtuse; 1 right + 2 obtuse + 1 acute; 2 obtuse + 2 acute; 4 right angles.

items.section_title: Faces, Edges, Corners — Observation and Classification
items.prompt: A cone has a curved surface and one flat face. Which label should go in the 'curved-faced shapes' group?

options.label: A
options.text: Cone

options.label: B
options.text: Cube

options.label: C
options.text: Square pyramid

options.label: D
options.text: Triangular prism

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Cone — it has a curved face (the lateral surface).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify which shape among the options has at least one curved face.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student does not distinguish flat from curved faces — a cube has only flat rectangular faces.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student confuses the pointed apex of a pyramid with a curved face.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student may focus on the shape's name (contains 'prism') without checking face type.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student handle a cone and run a finger over its surface to distinguish flat from curved; stretch: ask them to name one more shape that has a curved face.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Observe (border activity), p.5
exercise.description: Follow 5 instructions: colour rectangular-faced shapes red, add smileys to triangular-faced shapes, stars to curved-faced shapes, blue to shapes with no corner, circle shapes with same opposite faces.

items.section_title: Building and Drawing with Cubes
items.prompt: A partially drawn cube is shown on triangular dot paper. Two faces have been drawn. Complete the drawing by adding the remaining visible edges. How many edges does a cube have in total?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The student completes the cube by drawing the remaining edges connecting the dot-paper grid. A cube has 12 edges in total.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Follow the triangular dot-paper grid: connect the dots to complete each face, then count all edges.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student a cube model to look at while drawing; stretch: ask them to mark the hidden edges as dashed lines.

exercise.book_ref: Drawing Cubes on a Triangular Dot Paper, p.8
exercise.description: Complete the partially drawn cubes on triangular dot paper.

items.section_title: Angles — Introduction and Right Angles
items.prompt: Which of these shows an angle correctly marked?

options.label: A
options.text: A circle drawn at the endpoint of one line

options.label: B
options.text: A shaded region filling the interior of a triangle

options.label: C
options.text: A small arc drawn at the point where two lines meet

options.label: D
options.text: An arrow pointing along one of the lines

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A small arc at the vertex (meeting point) of two lines correctly marks an angle.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: An angle is marked by a small arc at the vertex where the two arms meet.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student confuses the interior region of a polygon with an individual angle.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student marks a direction rather than the opening between two arms.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student marks the endpoint of one arm rather than the vertex where both arms meet.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: show the student a drawn angle and demonstrate placing a small arc at the vertex; stretch: ask them to mark three different angles in a triangle drawing using arcs.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do Q1 (mark angles), p.10
exercise.description: Mark angles in five pictures (scissors, book corner, clock hands, etc.).

items.section_title: Acute and Obtuse Angles
items.prompt: A figure has three angles marked. Angle 1 is red, Angle 2 is green, Angle 3 is blue. Red = acute, Green = right angle, Blue = obtuse. Which colour-coding is correct?
items.visual_stimulus:
| Angle | Colour | Type |
| Angle 1 | Red | Acute |
| Angle 2 | Green | Right angle |
| Angle 3 | Blue | Obtuse |

options.label: A
options.text: Red for acute, green for obtuse, blue for right angle

options.label: B
options.text: Red for acute, green for right angle, blue for obtuse

options.label: C
options.text: Red for obtuse, green for acute, blue for right angle

options.label: D
options.text: Red for right angle, green for obtuse, blue for acute

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Red = acute, green = right angle, blue = obtuse — as stated in the task convention.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the colour code: acute → red, right angle → green, obtuse → blue.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Student has rotated all three colour-type pairings, indicating they did not read the convention.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student has swapped all three types without matching to the stated colours.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student correctly places red for acute but swaps green and blue for right angle and obtuse.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write the colour key on the board (red = acute, green = right, blue = obtuse) and let the student check each angle with the right-angle checker before colouring; stretch: ask them to draw a quadrilateral that would need all three colours.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do Q2 (colour-code angles), p.13
exercise.description: Mark acute angles in red, right angles in green, and obtuse angles in blue in given figures.

items.section_title: Puzzling Shapes and 2D Shape Sorting
items.prompt: Sort these shapes into three groups by number of sides: triangle, square, rectangle, pentagon, hexagon, circle. Write the name of each group and list the shapes in it.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 3 sides: triangle. 4 sides: square, rectangle. 5 or more sides / other: pentagon (5), hexagon (6), circle (0 — curved, no straight sides). Accept groupings with circle placed in a 'no straight sides' or 'special' group.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count straight sides for each shape and place it in the matching group.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw each shape and have the student count sides by pointing; stretch: ask the student to draw one more shape for each group that is not already listed.

exercise.book_ref: Card Game, p.20
exercise.description: Sort 2D-shape cards into three groups by number of sides; draw sorted shapes and explain sorting.

items.section_title: Let Us Try — Reasoning and Puzzle Tasks
items.prompt: Look at the four shapes below. Mark all the right angles in each shape with a small square. Then write the number of right angles next to each shape.
items.visual_stimulus:
| Shape | Description |
| Shape 1 | Rectangle |
| Shape 2 | Right-angled triangle |
| Shape 3 | Regular triangle (equilateral) |
| Shape 4 | Square |

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Shape 1 (rectangle): 4 right angles. Shape 2 (right-angled triangle): 1 right angle. Shape 3 (equilateral triangle): 0 right angles. Shape 4 (square): 4 right angles.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use a right-angle checker at each corner and mark with a small square if it matches; count and record.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide a paper right-angle checker and ask the student to test each corner before marking; stretch: ask which of the four shapes has only right angles and what name that property gives the shape.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Try Q8 (mark right angles), p.23
exercise.description: Mark right angles in each figure; write the number of right angles; identify shapes with only right angles.

items.section_title: Let Us Try — Reasoning and Puzzle Tasks
items.prompt: A model is to be built using exactly 9 straws as edges and 6 clay balls as corners. Using what you know about faces, edges, and corners of 3D shapes, name the solid that can be built, and explain how you worked it out.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Triangular prism. It has E = 9 edges and V = 6 corners. Check with F + V − E = 2: F = 2 − 6 + 9 = 5 faces. A triangular prism has 5 faces (2 triangles + 3 rectangles), 9 edges, and 6 corners. This matches.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use F + V − E = 2 to find F, then match E, V, F values to a known shape.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student the F + V − E = 2 rule and ask them to substitute V = 6 and E = 9 to find F, then look up which shape has those counts; stretch: ask them to identify the solid for 12 straws and 8 clay balls.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Try Q5 (model challenge), p.22
exercise.description: Make solid shape models using: (a) 12 straws + 8 clay balls; (b) 9 straws + 6 clay balls; (c) 15 straws + 10 clay balls; (d) 10 straws + 6 clay balls.
